## B. Account Terms

**Short version:** _Here's the guts of it. Personal Accounts and Organizations get different admin controls; a human has to create your Account, not a robot; you must be 13 or over; you need to hand over a valid email address; and you can't have more than one free Account. Greedy guts need not apply. You alone are on the hook for your Account and anything that happens while you're signed in to it or using it. And keeping your Account locked up tight? That's your job, mate._

### 1. Account Controls

* Users. Subject to these Terms, you keep ultimate admin control over your Personal Account and the Content in it. Your patch, your call.

* Organizations. The "owner" of an Organization that was set up under these Terms has ultimate admin control over that Organization and the Content in it: they're the boss cocky. Within the Service, an owner can manage User access to the Organization’s data and projects, so they decide who gets through the gate. An Organization can have more than one owner, but at least one Personal Account has to be named as an owner of an Organization. No ownerless mobs wandering about. And if you're the owner of an Organization under these Terms, we hold you responsible for whatever gets done on or through that Organization, so keep an eye on the troops.

### 2. Required Information

You must give us a valid email address to finish signing up, full stop. Anything else we ask for, like your real name, is up to you, unless you're accepting these terms on behalf of a legal entity (in which case we need more information about that legal entity), or you go for a [paid Account](#l-payment), in which case we'll need a bit more information to sort the billing.

### 3. Account Requirements

We've only got a few simple rules for Accounts on GitHub's Service. Nothing too curly.
* Only a human can create an Account. Accounts registered by "bots" or other automated methods aren't allowed, end of story. Mind you, we do allow machine accounts:
* A machine account is an Account set up by an individual human who accepts the Terms on behalf of the Account, gives a valid email address, and is responsible for whatever it gets up to. A machine account is used only for running automated tasks, nothing else. More than one user can steer a machine account, but at the end of the day the owner of the Account carries the can for what the machine does. You can keep no more than one free machine account on top of your free Personal Account.
* One person or legal entity can keep no more than one free Account (if you want to run a machine account as well, no worries, but it can only be used for running a machine).
* You've got to be 13 or older. Look, we're stoked to see bright young coders get keen as mustard on learning to program, but we have to comply with United States law. GitHub doesn't aim our Service at kids under 13, and we don't let any Users under 13 on our Service, full stop. If we find out about any User under the age of 13, we'll [terminate that User’s Account immediately](#m-cancellation-and-termination). No second chances. And if you live in a country outside the United States, your country's minimum age might be older; if so, it's on you to comply with your country's laws.
* Your login can only be used by one person — i.e., one login, one person, and you can't share it round a few people. A paid Organization can only give access to as many Personal Accounts as your subscription allows, so you get what you pay for.
* You can't use GitHub in breach of the export control or sanctions laws of the United States or any other applicable jurisdiction. You can't use GitHub if you are, or are working on behalf of, a [Specially Designated National (SDN)](https://www.treasury.gov/resource-center/sanctions/SDN-List/Pages/default.aspx) or a person subject to similar blocking or denied party prohibitions administered by a U.S. government agency. That's the serious end of things, no muckin' about. Mind you, GitHub may let persons in certain sanctioned countries or territories access certain GitHub services under U.S. government authorisations. For the full rundown, have a squiz at our [Export Controls policy](/site-policy/other-site-policies/github-and-trade-controls).
